Statement on Proposed Changes to Quarterly Reporting

Published 2026-10-06 11:00 UTC

Commissioner statement on proposed changes to quarterly reporting. Thank you, Chair. Today the Commission is proposing to give public companies the option to file semiannual reports instead of quarterly reports on Form 10-Q. I support issuing this proposal for public comment, and I want to explain why, as well as raise some questions I hope commenters will address.

Quarterly reporting has been required in the United States since 1970. Supporters argue that frequent disclosure keeps investors informed and markets efficient. Critics say it encourages managers to focus on short-term results at the expense of long-term investment, and that preparing quarterly reports imposes significant costs, especially on smaller companies.

The proposal would not eliminate interim disclosure. Companies choosing semiannual reporting would still be required to file current reports on Form 8-K when material events occur, and many would likely continue issuing quarterly earnings releases. The question is whether a full, reviewed set of financial statements every three months is necessary for all companies.

I am particularly interested in evidence from other markets. Several jurisdictions moved away from mandatory quarterly reporting over the past decade. Did companies in those markets invest more for the long term? Did information asymmetries grow, and did smaller investors lose out to those with better access to management?

I would also like commenters to address whether the option should be limited to smaller companies, how it would interact with stock exchange listing requirements, and whether investors need protections such as advance notice when a company changes its reporting frequency.

Thank you to the staff of the Division of Corporation Finance for their work on this proposal. I look forward to reviewing the comments.

Finally, I would encourage investors themselves to weigh in. The views of the people who rely on these reports should carry significant weight in our deliberations, and I hope the comment file reflects a broad range of perspectives, including from retail investors and smaller companies.
